demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
keep mind occupied all the time
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.explanation: The threat items are centered on assault/home-intrusion danger (noticing weapons, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of unexpected death of a loved one. Hypervigilance alone could fit PTSD broadly, but these two specific items imply a different trauma context.

Drop Responsibilities is framed as giving up responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers. In this profile, the listed triggers node is absent and the rest of the profile is dominated by grief/loss-linked appraisals and memory disturbance rather than a coherent pattern of situational avoidance for physical safety. That makes this specific strategy item poorly matched to the other selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring implies an ongoing interpersonal/home-invasion danger context. For trauma type of unexpected death of a loved one, this is hard to reconcile unless additional assault-related trauma is present. It also sits poorly with the formulation because Triggers→Threat is inactive, yet the threat content is highly specific to external intrusion rather than generalized post-loss threat.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is more consistent with trauma involving personal failure, assault, or injury than bereavement-focused PTSD. After unexpected death of a loved one, appraisals would more plausibly center on guilt, loss, permanent change, or the world being unsafe. 'I am a weak person' and 'I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me' are not impossible, but together they pull toward a different trauma formulation and are weakly anchored to the rest of the profile.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, the memory profile is largely grief/intrusion based, but 'Rage on Recall' stands out as difficult to reconcile with the rest of this profile because no other items indicate anger-focused appraisals, perpetrator blame, or threat-related meaning that would explain intense rage as the dominant recall response.

The Threat items describe a sustained current-danger state ('superalert', 'constantly tense and ready to react to danger'), but the formulation contains no active links into Threat and the other selected nodes are centered on loss, permanent change, numbing, and intrusive fragmented memory. This level of ongoing danger-readiness is not well integrated with the rest of the profile and appears clinically disconnected rather than supported by the appraisals or memory content.

vignette:
Adaeze is a 33-year-old African American woman who has worked as a park ranger for seven years, a role she once described as the truest expression of who she was - someone capable, grounded, and at home in the natural world. She is married and, until recently, was regarded by her supervisors as one of the most dependable rangers in her district. She presents now with a PCL-5 score of 46, seeking help approximately eight months after the sudden death of her younger brother, Emeka, who collapsed from an undetected cardiac arrhythmia during a family gathering. Adaeze was the first to reach him. She performed CPR for nearly twelve minutes while waiting for the ambulance, watching his face - so familiar, so still - and understanding, somewhere in the middle of those minutes, that she was losing him. He was twenty-nine.

In the weeks that followed, Adaeze found that the memory of that afternoon did not behave like a memory. It arrived in fragments without invitation - a sudden close-up of his lips, the texture of the grass beneath her knees, the sound her own voice made when she called his name - and then vanished before she could orient herself. At other moments the images were almost clinical in their precision, arriving with the flat, terrible clarity of photographs: Emeka's face at a particular angle, the exact position of his hands. When these fragments surfaced, they brought with them a grief so overwhelming that she could not function for minutes at a time, sometimes longer. She began to dread any moment of quiet, because stillness seemed to invite the images in. She stopped allowing herself to rest, stopped sitting without her phone or the radio on, filling every pause with noise or motion. What had begun as a response to the images gradually became a rule she enforced on herself: she must never be unoccupied.

This compulsion to stay mentally distracted had a direct cost to her work. The long stretches of solitary patrol that she had once treasured - walking fire roads through pine forest, monitoring trail conditions - became intolerable. She began delegating tasks she would normally have handled herself, calling in sick on days when she was assigned solo backcountry work, and quietly rerouting her patrol routes to stay near the visitor centre. Her supervisors noticed. A formal review was initiated two months ago, and Adaeze has not told her husband the full extent of what is happening at work.

Underlying all of this is what Adaeze has come to believe about herself since Emeka died. She is certain that she has been permanently altered - that whatever competence and steadiness once defined her has been destroyed, not temporarily disrupted. She feels, as she put it in the intake session, "like something that used to be a person." This conviction that she is no longer capable, that she is damaged beyond recovery, has made her less willing to attempt the very tasks that might challenge it. When she considers returning to solo patrol, or sitting quietly at home without distraction, she interprets the anticipated distress not as manageable difficulty but as confirmation of her permanent diminishment - and so she avoids. The avoidance, in turn, prevents her from processing what happened, and the memory remains raw and unintegrated, erupting without warning when her defences slip. Her body remains in a state of chronic readiness - tense, sleepless, scanning - and this physical alertness further convinces her that danger is still present, reinforcing her need to keep moving, keep busy, never stop.

The loop has tightened steadily. The more she avoids relaxation and drops her responsibilities, the less she encounters the memory in any controlled or tolerable way, and the more potent and intrusive it remains when it does arrive. Her sense of herself as permanently broken deepens with each retreat. She has begun to feel emotionally numb in the evenings, present in her marriage only in the most mechanical sense.

What finally brought her to seek help was her husband asking, quietly, whether she still wanted to be married to him. She does. She is most afraid that the answer she would give honestly - that she no longer knows who she is - means that nothing can be repaired.
